title: What Saved the American Bison
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history of the American bison (buffalo): the difference between bison and true buffalo, population estimates before European settlement, Native American buffalo jumps and hunting, the 19th-century Great Slaughter driven by hide hunting, railroads and government policy, the bison killing contests, and the founding of the American Bison Society and early protected herds. They then cover Ted Turner's bison ranches, the modern commercial bison industry and nutrition, brucellosis and Yellowstone culls, and inbreeding. The episode opens with Chuck's football anecdote and closes with a long listener-mail segment featuring comedian John Hodgman promoting his book That Is All, with tangents on regional sodas, wine, and end-of-the-world jokes.

segments.title: Opening banter and Chuck's football story
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck banter about a bison at a petting zoo, then Chuck recounts playing eighth-grade football for Beverly Elementary as a big lineman and making a sack and forced fumble.

segments.title: Bison vs. buffalo and species types
segments.summary: The hosts explain that American bison are native to North America while true buffalo are from Africa and Asia, trace the etymology of the word buffalo, and describe the wood bison and plains bison.

segments.title: Bison population numbers past and present
segments.summary: Current populations are described, including a 2007 census and about half a million in North America. Around 1889 only about 500 remained under federal protection. Estimates of pre-settlement populations range from 30 million (Shepard Krech III) to as high as 60 to 100 million, and the bison's size and speed are discussed.

segments.title: Apex predators and buffalo jumps
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the theory that Native American hunting shaped bison populations, then describe buffalo jumps, including Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump in Alberta, and the lemming myth.

segments.title: Native American hunting and bison overkill
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Comanche bison killing rates, the bison overkill debate about prehistoric extinctions, and how much bison a person needed per year.

segments.title: The Great Slaughter
segments.summary: Railroad expansion, the Winchester rifle and horses, hide demand in the East and Europe, and bison killing contests (including Thomas C. Nixon's record of 121 bison in 40 minutes) drove a mass slaughter. Hunting from trains and the government's aim to starve Plains Indians are also described.

segments.title: Early protection: American Bison Society and parks
segments.summary: Teddy Roosevelt and William Hornaday founded the American Bison Society in 1905. Herds were placed in the Bronx Zoo, Yellowstone, and the National Bison Range in Montana. Congress passed a law against poaching, but bison were never listed as endangered.

segments.title: Ted Turner and modern bison ranching
segments.summary: Ted Turner's bison ranches and his role in restoring herds are described. The hosts discuss the National Bison Association's standards, bison meat nutrition, and the commercial bison market, with about four thousand commercial bison in the US and Turner's roughly fifty thousand.

segments.title: Brucellosis, culls, and inbreeding
segments.summary: Brucellosis is described as a bacterial disease causing abortion in grazing animals, which leads to quarantines and culls, including about 3,700 bison shot outside Yellowstone over twenty years. Loss of habitat, the 1997 Yellowstone winter die-off, and inbreeding in small herds are also covered. Tribal herds are mentioned.

segments.title: Closing bison facts
segments.summary: The hosts note water buffalo milk versus bison, bison tail body-language signals, and point listeners to the HowStuffWorks article on bison extinction.

segments.title: John Hodgman book promotion and listener mail
segments.summary: John Hodgman appears as a hologram to promote his book That Is All, with tangents about regional sodas like Moxie-style brain drizzle and Chicko, his book tour, and end-of-the-world jokes. Listener mail is deferred to the following week.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts ask listeners to send listener mail and mention the Stuff from the Future video podcast, then sign off.
